newsitem.title: KENYA: African ministers weigh options against Burundi.
newsitem.headline: African ministers weigh options against Burundi.

text.p: African foreign ministers met behind closed doors in the Tanzanian capital Dar es Salaam on Tuesday to plot the next move against Burundi after the ruling army junta shunned talks with Hutu rebels.

Officials at the foreign ministry in Dar es Salaam told Reuters the ministers of Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, Zaire and Cameroun were meeting after Burundi defied regional leaders on Monday by refusing talks with rebels until economic sanctions are lifted.
"They are meeting behind closed doors. They will probably meet for the better part of the day," an official said by telephone.

Another one added: "The meeting is being held in view of Burundi's defiant response to the regional leaders. The ministers will have to come up with some kind of response to be presented to the heads of state for ratification."
The officials said the ministers would also consult with former Tanzanian president and Burundi mediator Julius Nyerere.

At their latest summit in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha on Saturday, the regional leaders gave Burundi one month to enter negotiations with Leonard Nyangoma's Forces for the Defence of Democracy (FDD) and smaller Hutu armed factions.

The leaders from Cameroun, Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda, Tanzania, Zambia, Zaire and the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) warned of penalties against any group in Burundi which refuses to negotiate within a month.
The leaders also refused to ease economic and transport sanctions against Burundi until strongman Major Pierre Buyoya began talks with rebels fighting his Tutsi military junta.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher urged East African leaders to consider easing the sanctions on Burundi during his recent tour of African countries.
The embargo was imposed on landlocked Burundi on July 31 as punishment for the military coup six days earlier which installed Buyoya.

Regional states, fearing the ethnic war between the rebels and the mainly Tutsi army is leading to catastrophe, justified the sanctions as a way to force the dominant Tutsi minority to share power with the Hutu majority.
Burundi Prime Minister Pascal Firmin Ndimira told diplomats on Monday: "The blockade is an obstacle and the government cannot dialogue until it is lifted."
Ndimira, a civilian and a Hutu, delivered a clear reply from Buyoya and the army colonels who backed him, saying sanctions were illegal, unfair and were causing a humanitarian crisis.
He said they imperilled the peace process by helping the rebels and he accused unspecified leaders of plotting against Burundi.

Killings by the rebels, the army, militias and even ordinary villagers occur every day in the tiny tea and coffee-growing central African state. Human rights and aid workers estimate the killings at 1,000 monthly and over 150,000 in the past three years, including a president and an archbishop.
Buyoya had previously agreed to unconditional talks with the rebels but Monday's change of heart seemed linked to his failure to get sanctions eased.
Sanctions are hitting Burundi hard. Exports of coffee and tea have virtually dried up and the regime is eating into its foreign reserves.
